title: Semisimplicity is equivalent to rational spanning by roots
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure] and $H$ a reductive $F$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme]. Use the maximal torus and root-datum conventions of [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure]: reductive means smooth, connected, affine and of finite type with no nontrivial smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup. Fix a split maximal torus $T$ in $H$, let $X=X^*(T)$, $X_*=X_*(T)$, and let $\Phi\subset X$ and $\Phi^\vee\subset X_*$ be the roots and coroots. Then $H$ is semisimple if and only if $\Phi$ spans $X\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q$. Here semisimple means having no nontrivial smooth connected solvable normal subgroup, and solvable means that successive commutator subgroup schemes become trivial. If these equivalent conditions hold, the rational extension of the integer pairing makes $(\Phi,\Phi^\vee)$ a finite reduced crystallographic root system in $X\otimes\mathbf Q$ and $X_*\otimes\mathbf Q$; in particular the coroots span the latter space.

source.place: Proposition 21.48, printed p.439; Appendix C.34--C.35, printed p.615; paragraph 22.9, printed p.465.

proof.text: Set $L=\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi}\mathbf Z\alpha$ and $M=X/L$. The lattice $X$ is free of finite rank by [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure], so its quotient $M$ is a finitely generated abelian group. By [lem-sfb-reductive-centre-root-quotient], $Z(H)=D_F(M)$ scheme-theoretically, with coordinate algebra having the basis $(e_m)_{m\in M}$. Consequently $Z(H)$ is finite over $F$ exactly when $M$ is finite: this is precisely finite-dimensionality of its coordinate algebra.

Apply [lem-sbc-finitely-generated-abelian-group-structure] to $M$ to write $M\simeq\mathbf Z^r\oplus C$ with $C$ finite (the finitely many prime-power cyclic factors). In particular $M$ is finite exactly when $r=0$, equivalently when $M$ is torsion. By [lem-sfb-diagonalizable-group-geometric-criteria], $D_F(M)\simeq\mathbf G_m^r\times D_F(C)$. If $r>0$, its first coordinate contains a nontrivial closed subtorus. If $r=0$, $Z(H)$ is finite by step 1, so any closed subtorus $S\simeq\mathbf G_m^s$ has finite-dimensional coordinate algebra: a closed immersion of affine schemes gives a surjection from the coordinate algebra of $Z(H)$. For $s>0$, the Laurent monomials $t_1^n$ for $n\in\mathbf Z$ are linearly independent, a contradiction. Thus $Z(H)$ has no nontrivial subtorus exactly when $M$ is finite. This includes $C$ with characteristic-primary torsion: $D_F(C)$ can be nonreduced, but is still finite.

source.place: Proof of Proposition 19.10, printed p.400; decomposition in Proposition 12.3, printed p.232.

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-reductive-radical-quotient], the radical $R(H)$ is the largest smooth connected normal solvable subgroup and is the largest subtorus of $Z(H)$. The solvability convention there (a finite normal series with commutative quotients) agrees with the commutator-series convention here: the derived subgroup lies in any normal subgroup with commutative quotient; induction places the successive derived subgroups in the successive terms of such a series. Conversely the derived series itself is such a series. Therefore $H$ is semisimple exactly when $R(H)=1$, exactly when $Z(H)$ has no nontrivial subtorus. By step 2 this is equivalent to finiteness of $M$. All hypotheses of the radical theorem hold because $F$ is algebraically closed and $H$ is smooth connected affine of finite type and reductive.

source.place: Proposition 19.10, printed p.400; Proposition 21.48, printed p.439.

proof.text: Finiteness of $M$ is equivalent to rational spanning. Indeed if $M$ is finite, each $x\in X$ has some positive multiple in $L$, so $x\otimes1$ is a rational linear combination of roots. Conversely, if the roots span $X\otimes\mathbf Q$, express each element $x_j$ of a finite integral basis of $X$ as a rational combination of roots and clear denominators to get $n_jx_j\in L$ with $n_j>0$. Equality in the rational space gives equality in $X$ because $X$ is free. The quotient $M$ is then generated by the images of the $x_j$, each of finite order dividing $n_j$, and is a quotient of the finite group $\prod_j\mathbf Z/n_j\mathbf Z$. Thus it is finite. Combined with step 3 this proves the stated equivalence, also in rank zero.

source.place: Definition C.34, printed p.615, and Proposition 21.48, printed p.439; denominator argument explicit.

proof.text: Extend the perfect integer pairing and the root datum of [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure] to $V=X\otimes\mathbf Q$ and $W=X_*\otimes\mathbf Q$. Choosing dual integral bases shows that the extended pairing is perfect; the lattice embeddings remain injective, and both reflection formulas remain valid by bilinearity. The index set is finite and the root-coroot pairings remain integers. Thus [lem-sfb-rational-root-coroot-span] applies. Under the equivalent conditions already proved, the roots span $V$, so that node gives that the coroots span $W$. Finiteness, nonzero roots, reducedness, the reflection permutations and crystallographic integrality are already part of the root datum and are preserved under rational extension (clear denominators for an equality between lattice vectors). These properties together with the two spanning assertions are exactly a finite reduced crystallographic root system in the paired spaces $V,W$. For $H=1$, both spaces and both families are empty or zero and the same argument applies.
